description: We are building AeroPulse at the NASA Space Apps Eindhoven Local Event—an interactive what-if urban heat-resilience digital twin that turns real NASA Earth observation data (Landsat 8/9 thermal LST, MODIS night-time LST, and NASA POWER irradiance/wind) plus CBS census demographics into neighbourhood-level cooling decisions.
summary:
AeroPulse is an interactive urban heat-resilience map that shows where cities get dangerously hot, who is most at risk there, and what would cool them down. Heat is uneven, with some streets several degrees hotter than others, and it hurts older people, people living alone and crowded areas the most. City averages hide this.

We combine real NASA data (Landsat 8/9 surface temperature, MODIS night-time temperature, NASA POWER sun and wind) with Sentinel-2 vegetation, census data and Meteomatics weather, all processed through Microsoft Planetary Computer. The result is a ranked list of neighbourhoods by heat risk. Sliders for trees, green roofs and cool pavements then show how much each area would cool, how many residents leave the high-risk group, and how much cooling energy is saved.

A physics-based model, cross-checked against the satellite data itself, drives the results. AeroPulse covers eight cities on three continents, uses only open data, and runs on free hosting, so any city can reuse it.
details:
What it does and how it works

AeroPulse is a static web app that works as a heat-resilience "digital twin" for eight cities: Eindhoven, Rotterdam, Amsterdam, Utrecht, The Hague, Berlin, Phoenix and Tokyo.

  1. Heat. A Python pipeline reads real NASA Landsat 8/9 thermal imagery (surface temperature) and NASA MODIS night-time temperature through the Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC API. It adds Sentinel-2 vegetation (NDVI) and ESA WorldCover built-up share and turns them into a heat grid per city.
  2. People. Census data (age 65+, single-person households, density) is combined with heat hazard into a risk score. Neighborhoods are ranked from most to least urgent.
  3. Solution. Sliders for tree canopy, green roofs and cool pavements run a first-order energy-balance model (albedo plus evapotranspiration). It is driven by live NASA POWER irradiance and wind and uses each city's albedo measured from Landsat. The map, ranking and KPIs update instantly.

Benefits and intended impact

City planners and climate officers can decide where to plant trees first and see what a plan buys before spending money. For Eindhoven, the maximum plan cools the hottest areas by about 3.7 °C, moves 87,000 residents out of elevated-risk areas and saves about 16 GWh a year of cooling energy. Residents and judges can see why heat is a fairness issue, not just a temperature one. Because it uses open data and free hosting, any city can copy it.

Tools used

  • Data: NASA Landsat, MODIS and POWER; ESA Sentinel-2 and WorldCover; CBS/PDOK, US Census and OpenStreetMap boundaries; Meteomatics weather (hottest day, forecast, PM2.5).
  • Pipeline: Python (pystac-client, odc-stac, rasterio, shapely, pyproj).
  • Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, Google Maps JavaScript API with a Leaflet fallback.
  • Hosting: Firebase Hosting (free tier), with a GitHub Actions job that refreshes the weather data and redeploys daily.
  • AI assistance: built with Claude (Anthropic) via Claude Code. The team reviewed and validated the work.

What is creative

  • It joins heat, people and solutions in one tool, instead of showing a temperature map alone.
  • A one-minute guided story explains the project in plain language, highlights parts of the screen, and lets visitors click and watch the map change.
  • The model checks itself against the satellite data, so it isn't just a black box.

Factors we considered

  • No synthesised data. Every map value comes from a real dataset. Where data is missing (aerosol optical depth, population for Berlin and Tokyo) the app says "n/a" or shows hazard-only risk.
  • Validation. A regression on real satellite cells explains 72–90% of surface-temperature variance in the Dutch cities. Physics-based and satellite-based vegetation cooling agree within a factor of 1.7.
  • Known weaknesses, addressed: Landsat's morning snapshot is complemented by MODIS night data (night heat island +0.7 to +3 K). The vulnerability index is tested for rank stability and labelled a proxy, not a health-validated measure. Meteomatics PM2.5 stands in for aerosol data. Albedo is measured per city (0.13 in Dutch cities, 0.21 in Phoenix) rather than assumed. The app covers three continents.
  • Security and cost. API credentials stay out of the browser, and the whole system runs free.
  • Limits: it's a planning tool for comparing options, not an exact forecast.
